questions.title: The parameter that turns the quadratic into a straight line
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 2.6 (the quadratic function f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c: its graph, vertex, axis of symmetry and discriminant)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The leading coefficient carries the parameter, so the curve silently changes type at one special value of m.
questions.question: For each real number $m$, define $f(x)=(m-1)x^{2}+2(m+1)x+(m+2)$. The family of curves $y=f(x)$ changes character as $m$ varies, and several parts of this question ask you to describe that change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that when $m=1$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is a straight line, and state its equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For $m\neq1$, find the coordinates of the vertex of $y=f(x)$, giving your answer in terms of $m$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the set of values of $m$ for which the graph of $y=f(x)$ does not meet the $x$-axis.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why, for every $m>1$, the vertex lies below the $x$-axis, and deduce the number of real roots of $f(x)=0$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Setting $m=1$ makes the coefficient of $x^{2}$ equal to zero, so the quadratic degenerates to a linear expression **(M1)**. Substituting gives $f(x)=2(1+1)x+(1+2)=4x+3$ **(A1)**. Hence the graph is the straight line $y=4x+3$ **(A1)** *(AG)*. The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is the only term that can vanish, so this is the single value at which the family changes type.

**(b)** Completing the square for $m\neq1$, write $f(x)=(m-1)\left[x^{2}+\frac{2(m+1)}{m-1}x\right]+(m+2)$ **(M1)**. The bracket becomes $\left(x+\frac{m+1}{m-1}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{m+1}{m-1}\right)^{2}$ **(A1)**, so the axis of symmetry is $x=-\frac{m+1}{m-1}$ **(A1)**. Substituting this value and simplifying gives $-\frac{m+3}{m-1}$ **(M1)(A1)**. The vertex is therefore $\left(-\frac{m+1}{m-1},-\frac{m+3}{m-1}\right)$. This is the standard vertex formula for a parabola, and it is valid for every value of $m$ except the one excluded by the question.

**(c)** The discriminant is $[2(m+1)]^{2}-4(m-1)(m+2)$ **(M1)** $=4(m+1)^{2}-4(m-1)(m+2)$ **(A1)** $=4(m+3)$ **(A1)**. The graph misses the $x$-axis exactly when the discriminant is negative, so $4(m+3)<0$ **(M1)**, giving $m<-3$ **(A1)**. Because the discriminant is linear in $m$, its sign changes at exactly one value, so the set of such $m$ is a single ray rather than a bounded interval.

**(d)** For $m>1$ the leading coefficient $m-1$ is positive, so the parabola opens upwards **(A1)**. The $y$-coordinate of the vertex is $-\frac{m+3}{m-1}$, and both $m+3$ and $m-1$ are positive, so this value is negative **(R1)**. An upward parabola whose vertex lies below the $x$-axis must cross the axis twice **(M1)**, so $f(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots **(A1)**, consistent with $4(m+3)>0$. The sign of the discriminant gives independent confirmation of this count, so the number of real roots is exactly two.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The intended observation is that $m=1$ removes the $x^{2}$ term. Accept any statement that the graph has degree one. A candidate who substitutes $m=1$, writes $f(x)=4x+3$ and states the equation of the line earns all three marks; the word 'straight' is not required if the equation is given.

(b) The (M1) is for an honest attempt at completing the square, or for using $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$. The (A1) for the axis is independent, so a candidate with a correct $x$-coordinate but an arithmetic slip in the $y$-coordinate keeps the axis mark. Accept the vertex written in any equivalent algebraic form.

(c) Award (M1) for a correct discriminant expression even if the simplification is wrong. The final (A1) requires the strict inequality $m<-3$; writing $m\le-3$ forfeits it, because at $m=-3$ the curve is tangent to the axis and does meet it.

(d) This part tests reasoning rather than computation. The (R1) requires both signs to be justified. A candidate who says only that the vertex is below the axis, without saying that the parabola opens upwards, cannot reach the conclusion. Follow through from an incorrect vertex in (b) is allowed here.

**Extension:** the case $m<-3$ gives no real roots, while $-3<m<1$ gives two roots, and $m=1$ gives one.
questions.explanation:
The trap is that the leading coefficient depends on the parameter. Most candidates treat $f$ as a quadratic throughout, and part (a) is designed to catch exactly that: when $m=1$ there is no $x^{2}$ term at all, and the curve is a line. A candidate who divides by $m-1$ without first checking that $m\neq1$ will produce an undefined vertex.

The second trap is the discriminant. Expanding $[2(m+1)]^{2}-4(m-1)(m+2)$ is routine, but the cancellation is delicate: the $m^{2}$ terms disappear and leave the linear expression $4(m+3)$. Candidates who lose a factor of four, or who expand $(m-1)(m+2)$ carelessly, will get the wrong threshold. The correct reading is that the sign of the discriminant is controlled entirely by $m+3$, so the boundary is at $m=-3$, not at $m=1$ or $m=0$.

Part (d) is a reasoning question that rewards understanding the shape of a parabola. The vertex formula from part (b) is reused, but the point is not to compute anything new: it is to notice that an upward-opening parabola whose lowest point is below the axis has to cross the axis on both sides. The discriminant from part (c) confirms this, since $m>1$ makes $4(m+3)$ positive.

Classic wrong turns include assuming the family is always a parabola; writing the vertex with the wrong signs; treating 'does not meet the $x$-axis' as 'discriminant less than or equal to zero'; and in part (d) concluding that there are no real roots because the vertex is negative. A candidate who sketches the family for two or three values of $m$ will see the transition from a line at $m=1$ to very narrow parabolas for values of $m$ close to one. The family is a useful illustration of how a single parameter can change the nature of a curve.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 2.6 bullet on the quadratic function and its discriminant. The lever is the parameter m placed in every coefficient, including the leading one, so that the family changes type at m = 1 and the discriminant collapses to the linear expression 4(m+3); those specific coefficients were chosen so that the no-intersection condition is m < -3 and the root count for m > 1 follows from the sign of the vertex rather than from a formula.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed numerically in Python: the vertex formula was tested at m = 0, 2 and 5 against direct substitution, and the discriminant 4(m+3) was checked at several values of m.

questions.title: An inequality that holds only for a range of its own parameter
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 2.7 (solution of quadratic equations and inequalities) and SL 2.6 (the quadratic function and its discriminant)
questions.subtopic: 2.7 Solution of quadratic equations and inequalities and 2.6 The quadratic function
questions.challenge_mechanism: The expression is positive for all x only when a discriminant condition and a leading-coefficient condition agree at the same boundary.
questions.question: For each real number $k$, define $E(x)=(k+1)x^{2}-2(k+2)x+(k+5)$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the discriminant of $E(x)$ is equal to $-8k-4$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the set of values of $k$ for which $E(x)>0$ for every real number $x$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the values of $x$ satisfying $E(x)>0$ when $k=-1$, where $E$ is no longer quadratic.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the value of $k$ for which $E(x)=0$ has exactly one real solution, and state that solution.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Here $a=k+1$, $b=-2(k+2)$ and $c=k+5$, so the discriminant is $b^{2}-4ac$ **(M1)** $=4(k+2)^{2}-4(k+1)(k+5)$ **(A1)**. Expanding, $(k+2)^{2}=k^{2}+4k+4$ and $(k+1)(k+5)=k^{2}+6k+5$ **(A1)**, so the discriminant equals $4[(k^{2}+4k+4)-(k^{2}+6k+5)]=4(-2k-1)=-8k-4$ **(A1)** *(AG)*. The $k^{2}$ terms cancel, which is why the discriminant is linear in $k$ rather than quadratic, and this feature is what makes the later parts tractable.

**(b)** For $E(x)>0$ for every real $x$ the parabola must open upwards and have no real roots, so $a>0$ and the discriminant must be negative **(M1)**. The discriminant $-8k-4$ is negative precisely when $-8k<4$, that is $k>-\frac{1}{2}$ **(A1)(A1)**. For such values $k+1>\frac{1}{2}>0$, so the leading coefficient is automatically positive **(R1)**, and the condition is exactly $k>-\frac{1}{2}$ **(A1)**. No separate condition on $k$ is required beyond the discriminant inequality, because the boundary value of $k$ is greater than minus one and therefore keeps the leading coefficient positive.

**(c)** When $k=-1$ the coefficient of $x^{2}$ vanishes, so $E(x)=-2x+4$ **(M1)(A1)**. Then $-2x+4>0$ gives $x<2$ **(A1)**. The inequality is strict, so the endpoint $x=2$ is excluded and the solution set is the open ray to the left of two.

**(d)** A repeated root occurs when the discriminant is zero, so $-8k-4=0$ and $k=-\frac{1}{2}$ **(M1)(A1)**. Substituting, $E(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x+\frac{9}{2}=\frac{1}{2}(x-3)^{2}$ **(A1)**, so the single solution is $x=3$ **(A1)**. The completed square shows that the expression is non-negative for every real $x$, and it is equal to zero only at the single point just found. The three answers form a consistent picture: below the boundary the expression is always positive, at the boundary it touches zero once, and beyond the boundary it changes sign.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for quoting $b^{2}-4ac$ with the correct coefficients. The expansion marks are independent: a candidate who expands correctly but makes a sign slip while collecting terms can still earn the first two. The final (A1) requires the exact form $-8k-4$; the unsimplified $4(-2k-1)$ is acceptable.

(b) The key is that 'positive for every real $x$' is a two-condition statement. A candidate who only requires the discriminant to be negative reaches $k>-\frac{1}{2}$, which happens to be correct, but the (R1) is awarded only if the leading coefficient is also verified. Award full marks to a candidate who argues that the discriminant condition already forces $k+1>0$.

(c) This is a deliberate degenerate case. The (M1) is for recognising that the quadratic term disappears, the (A1) for the correct linear expression, and the final (A1) for the strict inequality $x<2$. Do not accept $x\le2$.

(d) The (M1) is for setting the discriminant to zero and the (A1) for $k=-\frac{1}{2}$. Completing the square earns the third mark and the value $x=3$ the fourth. A candidate who uses the quadratic formula and obtains the double root earns full credit.

**Note:** the boundary value $k=-\frac{1}{2}$ belongs to (d) rather than (b), since there $E$ has a zero.
questions.explanation:
The item is built around a single expression whose sign behaviour changes at two different parameter values. Part (a) is mechanical but sets up everything: the discriminant is linear in $k$, which is unusual for a quadratic family and is what makes the later parts tractable. Candidates who expect a quadratic discriminant and try to factor it waste time.

Part (b) is where the reasoning lives. The phrase 'for every real $x$' requires two separate conditions: the parabola must open upwards and must not touch the axis. Many candidates remember only the discriminant condition. Here the trap is benign, because the discriminant condition $k>-\frac{1}{2}$ already implies $k+1>0$, but the mark scheme rewards the candidate who notices this rather than one who assumes it. A candidate who writes $k>-\frac{1}{2}$ with no justification loses the reasoning mark.

Part (c) breaks the family. Setting $k=-1$ removes the quadratic term, and the expression becomes the decreasing line $-2x+4$. Candidates who blindly apply the discriminant to a line will divide by zero. This part exists to test whether the algebra is being watched.

Part (d) reuses the discriminant at its zero. The double root at $x=3$ is the natural bridge between the strict inequality of part (b) and the degenerate case of part (c). The classic errors are forgetting that $a>0$ is required in part (b); solving $-2x+4>0$ as $x>2$; and treating the repeated root as two coincident solutions. Plotting the family for a negative value of $k$ shows the parabola crossing the axis twice, which is precisely the case that the inequality in part (b) is designed to exclude. A useful sanity check is that the expression is a perfect square at the boundary, so its sign never becomes negative.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 2.7 bullet on quadratic inequalities together with the SL 2.6 discriminant. The lever is a parameter k in all three coefficients, tuned so that the discriminant is the linear expression -8k-4; this makes the positivity condition k > -1/2 coincide with the leading-coefficient condition, and the value k = -1 collapses the expression to a line so that the quadratic machinery has to be abandoned rather than extended.

verification.method: The discriminant -8k-4 was recomputed algebraically and evaluated at k = 0, 1, -1 and -1/2, and the repeated-root case was verified by expanding (1/2)(x-3)^2.

questions.title: Two curves that are reflections, and the range of k that keeps both roots
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 2.9 (exponential functions and their graphs, including the asymptote and the relationship between y = a^x and y = (1/a)^x) and SL 2.10 (solving equations analytically)
questions.subtopic: 2.9 Exponential functions and their graphs and 2.10 Solving equations analytically
questions.challenge_mechanism: Two mirror-image curves hide a substitution that forces both roots of a quadratic to be positive.
questions.question: Let $f(x)=3^{x}$ and $g(x)=3^{-x}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sketch the graphs of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ on the same axes, stating the equation of the asymptote and the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the graph of $y=g(x)$ is the reflection of the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the $y$-axis, and find the coordinates of their point of intersection.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the two transformations that map the graph of $y=f(x)$ onto the graph of $y=3^{x-2}+1$, and state the equation of the asymptote and the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of the image.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the set of values of $k$ for which $3^{2x}-4\cdot3^{x}+k=0$ has two distinct real solutions.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Both curves have the negative $x$-axis as a horizontal asymptote, that is $y=0$ **(A1)**. Since $3^{0}=1$, both pass through $(0,1)$ **(A1)**. The graph of $f$ rises from left to right without bound, while the graph of $g$ falls from left to right, tending to zero **(A1)(A1)**. Both curves lie entirely above the $x$-axis, so neither ever meets it, and the only point they share is the intercept.

**(b)** Replacing $x$ by $-x$ in $f$ gives $f(-x)=3^{-x}=g(x)$ **(M1)(A1)**, so $g$ is the reflection of $f$ in the $y$-axis. At an intersection $3^{x}=3^{-x}$ **(M1)**, so $3^{2x}=1$ and hence $x=0$ **(A1)**; the point is $(0,1)$. The reflection is a symmetry of this particular pair of curves, and it does not depend on the value of the base.

**(c)** We have $3^{x-2}+1=f(x-2)+1$. The graph of $f(x-2)$ is obtained by translating $y=f(x)$ by $2$ units in the positive $x$-direction **(A1)**, and adding $1$ translates the result by $1$ unit in the positive $y$-direction **(A1)**. The asymptote $y=0$ moves to $y=1$ **(A1)**, and the $y$-intercept is $3^{0-2}+1=\frac{1}{9}+1=\frac{10}{9}$, that is $\left(0,\frac{10}{9}\right)$ **(A1)**. Because both operations are translations, their order is immaterial, and the image is the same curve either way.

**(d)** Put $u=3^{x}$, so $u>0$ and the equation becomes $u^{2}-4u+k=0$ **(M1)**. Two distinct real solutions in $x$ require two distinct positive roots $u$ **(R1)**. The discriminant $16-4k$ must be positive, giving $k<4$ **(M1)(A1)**, and the product of the roots, equal to $k$, must be positive, giving $k>0$ **(A1)**. Hence $0<k<4$ **(A1)**. The product condition is the one that is easily overlooked, and it is what removes the negative values of $k$ from the answer.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The sketch need not be to scale, but both curves must show the correct shape: one increasing, one decreasing, both passing through $(0,1)$ and both asymptotic to the $x$-axis. Award the asymptote mark for $y=0$ and the intercept mark for $(0,1)$. A candidate who draws only one curve cannot earn more than two of the four marks.

(b) The (M1) is for the substitution $x\mapsto-x$, and the (A1) for identifying it as a reflection in the $y$-axis. The intersection mark is independent: award it for any correct argument, including equating indices.

(c) The order of the two translations does not matter here, because both are translations. Accept a translation of $2$ to the right and $1$ up in either order. The asymptote of the image is $y=1$, not $y=0$. The $y$-intercept must be exact; a decimal such as $1.11$ forfeits the final (A1).

(d) The (R1) is the crucial mark: it is not enough that the quadratic in $u$ has two distinct roots, because $u=3^{x}$ must be positive. A candidate who gives only $k<4$ has forgotten the positivity of $u$. Follow through from a correct discriminant in an otherwise wrong part.

**Extension:** for $k\le0$ exactly one root is positive, so the original equation has exactly one real solution.
questions.explanation:
The question concerns two exponential curves that are mirror images of each other, but the difficulty is concentrated in the final part, where a hidden quadratic in $3^{x}$ appears. Parts (a) to (c) are standard graph work and are there to establish the vocabulary of asymptote, intercept and transformation before the algebraic twist.

The most common error is in part (d). Candidates set the discriminant of $u^{2}-4u+k=0$ to be positive, obtain $k<4$, and stop. That is necessary but not sufficient: the substitution $u=3^{x}$ restricts $u$ to positive values, so both roots of the quadratic must be positive. For a quadratic with leading coefficient one, the product of the roots equals $k$, so positivity of the product gives $k>0$. The sum of the roots is $4$, which is positive automatically, so no further condition is needed. The answer is therefore the open interval $0<k<4$.

A candidate who reasons only about the discriminant will include negative values of $k$ in the answer. At $k=-1$, for instance, the quadratic $u^{2}-4u-1=0$ has one positive and one negative root, and only the positive root corresponds to a real $x$, so there is exactly one solution rather than two. This is the fastest numerical check.

Other traps include treating the asymptote of $3^{x-2}+1$ as $y=0$; computing the $y$-intercept as $3^{-2}$ and forgetting the $+1$; and in part (b) assuming the curves meet where the graph crosses the axis. The base three is a red herring, since every positive base other than one behaves in the same way and the structure of the answer does not depend on it. The base is arbitrary, so the result is really a statement about all exponential functions whose base is greater than one.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 2.9 bullet on exponential functions and the reflection relation between y = a^x and y = (1/a)^x, together with the SL 2.10 bullet on analytic solution. The lever is the substitution u = 3^x in a later part, where the positivity of u converts a discriminant condition into a product-of-roots condition; the coefficients 4 and k were chosen so that the boundary k < 4 and the positivity boundary k > 0 give the clean interval 0 < k < 4.

verification.method: The y-intercept 10/9, the reflection point (0, 1) and the root conditions for u^2 - 4u + k = 0 were recomputed numerically in Python at k = 0, 1, 4 and 5.

questions.title: A quadratic in disguise whose two roots must both be positive
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 2.10 (solving equations, both graphically and analytically, including equations of the form e^(2x) - 5e^x + 4 = 0) and SL 2.9 (exponential functions and their graphs)
questions.subtopic: 2.10 Solving equations, both graphically and analytically and 2.9 Exponential functions and their graphs
questions.challenge_mechanism: The substitution replaces the variable by a positive quantity, so the discriminant test alone cannot decide how many roots survive.
questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=e^{2x}-5e^{x}+4$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the substitution $u=e^{x}$ reduces the equation $f(x)=0$ to $u^{2}-5u+4=0$, and hence solve $f(x)=0$ exactly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the set of values of $k$ for which $e^{2x}-5e^{x}+k=0$ has no real solutions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Solve the inequality $f(x)>0$, giving your answer in exact form.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the exact minimum value of $f(x)$ and the value of $x$ at which it occurs.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Since $e^{2x}=(e^{x})^{2}$, writing $u=e^{x}$ turns $f(x)=0$ into $u^{2}-5u+4=0$ **(M1)(A1)**. Factorising, $(u-1)(u-4)=0$, so $u=1$ or $u=4$ **(A1)**. Because $u=e^{x}$, this gives $e^{x}=1$ or $e^{x}=4$, that is $x=0$ or $x=\ln 4$ **(A1)**. Both values of $u$ are positive, so both survive the substitution and give genuine real solutions for $x$.

**(b)** With $u=e^{x}>0$ the equation is $u^{2}-5u+k=0$ **(M1)**. If the discriminant $25-4k$ is negative the quadratic has no real roots, so there is no positive $u$ and hence no real $x$ **(A1)(M1)**. This requires $25-4k<0$, that is $k>\frac{25}{4}$ **(A1)**. Conversely, for $k\le\frac{25}{4}$ the quadratic has at least one positive root, so real solutions exist; the answer is $k>\frac{25}{4}$. The converse direction is needed to show that no value of $k$ below the threshold can be added to the set.

**(c)** The inequality $f(x)>0$ becomes $u^{2}-5u+4>0$, that is $(u-1)(u-4)>0$ **(M1)(A1)**, so $u<1$ or $u>4$ **(A1)**. Translating back, $e^{x}<1$ or $e^{x}>4$, so $x<0$ or $x>\ln 4$ **(A1)**. The two rays are disjoint, so the solution set is not an interval but the union of two separate pieces.

**(d)** Completing the square in $u$, $u^{2}-5u+4=\left(u-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{9}{4}$ **(M1)(A1)**, so the least value is $-\frac{9}{4}$ **(A1)**. This is attained when $u=\frac{5}{2}$, and since $\frac{5}{2}>0$ this corresponds to a real $x$ with $x=\ln\frac{5}{2}$ **(A1)**. The positivity of the location is what guarantees that the stationary point of the quadratic is actually reached by the exponential curve, so the value is a true minimum rather than a lower bound.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for recognising that $e^{2x}$ is the square of $e^{x}$; the (A1) is for the reduced quadratic. Any correct method of solving it is accepted, including the formula. The final (A1) requires both exact roots $x=0$ and $x=\ln4$; a decimal approximation is not sufficient.

(b) The (M1) is for the substitution and the (A1) for the discriminant. The second (M1) is for the reasoning that a negative discriminant means no real $u$, and the final (A1) for the strict inequality $k>\frac{25}{4}$. Candidates who write $k\ge\frac{25}{4}$ forfeit the final mark, because at that value there is a repeated positive root and therefore one real solution.

(c) Award (M1) for the factorisation and (A1) for the sign analysis $u<1$ or $u>4$. The two translation marks are for converting the inequalities back to inequalities in $x$. Accept $\ln4$ written as $2\ln2$.

(d) The (M1) is for completing the square or differentiating; the (A1) for the completed square. The minimum value must be exact, and the location must be justified by noting that $u=\frac{5}{2}$ is positive. A candidate who reports the minimum value but not its location earns three of the four marks.

**Extension:** the range of $f$ is $\left[-\frac{9}{4},\infty\right)$.
questions.explanation:
This is the classic quadratic in disguise, but the question pushes past the standard version by asking for a parameter range and an exact minimum. The disguise is the point: $e^{2x}-5e^{x}+4$ looks like an exponential expression, yet the substitution $u=e^{x}$ makes it a quadratic. The whole question turns on remembering that $u$ is constrained to be positive.

Part (a) is routine once the substitution is seen. Part (b) is the subtle one. A candidate who requires only that the discriminant be negative obtains $k>\frac{25}{4}$ and is right, but for the wrong reason: they have not checked that the absence of real roots of the quadratic is enough. It is enough, because a negative discriminant means no real $u$ at all, positive or otherwise. The converse direction is what needs care, and the answer justifies it through the product of the roots.

Part (c) is a sign question. The factorisation $(u-1)(u-4)>0$ gives a union of two rays, not an interval. A candidate who writes $1<u<4$ has the sign backwards. Translating back to $x$ uses the fact that $e^{x}$ is increasing, so the inequalities are preserved.

Part (d) is an optimisation in the $u$-variable. The vertex of the quadratic is at $u=\frac{5}{2}$, which is positive, so the minimum of the quadratic is actually attained by the exponential function. This check is essential: had the vertex been at a negative value of $u$, the minimum of $f$ would not occur. A candidate who sketches the graph will see that the curve dips below the axis between the two roots and returns above it afterwards, which is exactly the sign pattern recorded in part (c). The value is attained, not merely approached, because the required value of the substituted variable is positive.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 2.10 bullet on solving equations analytically, including the standard e^(2x) - 5e^x + 4 = 0 example, paired with SL 2.9. The lever is the requirement that u = e^x be positive, which turns the discriminant test in part (b) and the optimisation in part (d) into genuine checks; the coefficients 5 and 4 were kept so that the roots are 1 and 4 and the minimum sits at u = 5/2 with value -9/4.

verification.method: The roots, the parameter threshold 25/4 and the minimum -9/4 were recomputed numerically in Python by evaluating f at x = 0, ln 4, ln 2 and ln(5/2).

questions.title: A stretch and a translation that do not commute
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 2.11 (transformations of graphs: translations, stretches and reflections, and the effect of the order in which they are applied)
questions.challenge_mechanism: A horizontal stretch and a horizontal translation produce the same graph only when their order and distance are tracked together.
questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^{2}-4x+5$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find $f(x)$ in the form $(x-h)^{2}+k$ and state the coordinates of the vertex of $y=f(x)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the graph of $y=f(2x-6)$ as a combination of a horizontal stretch and a horizontal translation of the graph of $y=f(x)$, and explain why the translation is $6$ units in one order and $3$ units in the other.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the vertex of $y=f(2x-6)$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Solve the equation $f(2x-6)=f(x)$, giving both solutions in exact form.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Completing the square, $f(x)=x^{2}-4x+4+1=(x-2)^{2}+1$ **(M1)(A1)**. Comparing with $(x-h)^{2}+k$ gives $h=2$ and $k=1$ **(A1)**, so the vertex is $(2,1)$ **(A1)**. The completed-square form is the most convenient way to read off the vertex, and it will be reused in the later parts.

**(b)** Factorising the argument, $f(2x-6)=f(2(x-3))$ **(M1)**. Starting from $y=f(x)$, a horizontal stretch of scale factor $\frac{1}{2}$ about the $y$-axis replaces $x$ by $2x$ and gives $y=f(2x)$ **(A1)**, and translating the result $3$ units in the positive $x$-direction replaces $x$ by $x-3$, giving $y=f(2(x-3))=f(2x-6)$ **(A1)**. In the other order, translating first by $6$ units gives $y=f(x-6)$ **(M1)**, and then stretching by factor $\frac{1}{2}$ replaces $x$ by $2x$, giving $y=f(2x-6)$ **(A1)**. The translation distances differ because the stretch acts on the translation itself: $2(x-3)=2x-6$, so a translation of $3$ before the stretch corresponds to a translation of $6$ after it. Both descriptions end at the same curve, and the discrepancy in the translation distance is the whole content of the part.

**(c)** Substituting into the completed-square form, $f(2x-6)=(2x-6-2)^{2}+1=(2x-8)^{2}+1=4(x-4)^{2}+1$ **(M1)(A1)**. Hence the vertex is $(4,1)$ **(A1)(A1)**. The vertex has the same height as before, which is expected because the stretch and the translation are both horizontal.

**(d)** Setting the two expressions equal, $4x^{2}-32x+65=x^{2}-4x+5$ **(M1)**, so $3x^{2}-28x+60=0$ **(A1)**. The quadratic formula gives $x=\frac{28\pm\sqrt{784-720}}{6}=\frac{28\pm8}{6}$ **(A1)**, so the required solutions are $x=6$ or $x=\frac{10}{3}$. The two roots are the points at which the original parabola and its horizontally transformed copy have the same height. A quick check confirms that both values satisfy the simplified quadratic and that their sum and product match the coefficients.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for an attempt at completing the square, and the (A1) for the correct completed-square form. The vertex marks are independent of the algebraic form: a candidate who reads the vertex directly from a correct graph earns them. Accept the form written with the square completed in an equivalent way.

(b) This is a description question, so the marks are for the structure of the argument. The (M1) is for factoring out the $2$; the two (A1) marks are for the stretch-then-translate route; the (M1)(A1) pair is for the translate-then-stretch route. A candidate who gives only one route can earn at most three of the five marks. The final explanation must connect the two distances through $2(x-3)=2x-6$.

(c) The (M1) is for substituting $2x-6$ into the function, and the (A1) for reaching $4(x-4)^{2}+1$. The vertex marks require the coordinates in the correct order. A candidate who writes $(1,4)$ forfeits both.

(d) The (M1) is for equating the two expressions and the (A1) for the simplified quadratic. The final (A1) requires both roots; a candidate who gives only $x=6$ earns two of the three marks. Accept $\frac{10}{3}$ written as $3\frac{1}{3}$.

**Extension:** the same two roots arise from $(2x-8)^{2}=(x-2)^{2}$.
questions.explanation:
The question looks like routine graph transformation, but the two orders in part (b) do not produce the same intermediate graph, and the reason is the whole point. A horizontal stretch by factor $\frac{1}{2}$ and a horizontal translation of $3$ units combine to give $f(2(x-3))$, whereas translating $6$ units first and then stretching gives the same final graph. The two descriptions are both correct because the stretch acts on whatever translation has already been applied.

The trap is to assume that transformations always commute. They do not: a horizontal translation and a horizontal stretch fail to commute unless the translation is zero. A candidate who writes 'stretch by $\frac{1}{2}$ then translate $6$' will produce the wrong intermediate expression, because the translation they have described belongs to the other stage. The mark scheme rewards the candidate who keeps the two orders separate and states the correct distance for each.

Part (c) is a straightforward substitution but is easy to get wrong if the completed-square form is not used. Expanding $f(2x-6)$ directly gives $4x^{2}-32x+65$, and completing the square on that expression is slower and more error-prone. Reading the vertex off the transformed form is the intended route.

Part (d) is an algebraic intersection problem. The two quadratics share the same $y$-intercept, which is why one root is far to the right and the other lies between $3$ and $4$. A candidate who tries to solve graphically without a calculator will struggle to locate $\frac{10}{3}$ precisely. The clean route is to cancel the $+1$ and take square roots, or to expand and use the formula, as shown. The base function was chosen so that both the vertex and the intersection points are simple fractions, which makes the transformation behaviour easy to check by hand.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 2.11 bullet on transformations of graphs and the order in which they are applied. The lever is the argument 2x - 6 rewritten as 2(x - 3), which forces the solver to state a 1/2 stretch with a 3-unit translation in one order and a 6-unit translation in the other; the base function x^2 - 4x + 5 was chosen so that the transformed vertex (4, 1) and the intersection roots 6 and 10/3 come out exactly.

verification.method: The completed square, the transformed vertex (4, 1) and the roots 6 and 10/3 were recomputed numerically in Python by direct substitution into both sides of f(2x-6) = f(x).
